author: Philip K. Dick
card_summary: One of PKD's early realist novels—written in the early 1950s but not published until 2007—following a discontented young television salesman in postwar California as he drifts through disillusionment, infidelity, and a search for meaning; mainstream fiction, with no science-fictional element.
page_summary:
Stuart Hadley is a young appliance and television salesman in a Bay Area town in the early 1950s, married and outwardly settled but corroded by restlessness and contempt for the ordinary life he is living. Over the course of the novel he drifts through an affair, a flirtation with a charismatic religious movement, drinking, self-destruction, and a groping search for some authenticity beneath the surface of consumer prosperity, before arriving at a chastened accommodation with the world he tried to escape.

This is Dick working in the realist, mainstream mode he pursued seriously in the 1950s and largely failed to sell—no aliens, no alternate worlds, just the disillusionment and quiet desperation of postwar American domestic life. The themes that would drive his science fiction are already here in naturalistic form: alienation, the hollowness of suburban prosperity, the hunger for meaning, and the pull of a movement promising transcendence. It offers a clear view of the everyday register beneath the metaphysics of his genre work.

Long unpublished, the manuscript appeared only in 2007, a quarter-century after Dick's death, as the last of his surviving early mainstream novels to reach print. It is of primary interest as biography and as the naturalistic bedrock from which his more famous fiction grew.
